subject: Coffee & Tea
title: First Wave: Mass Production
description: A 60-second lesson on First Wave: Mass Production.

hook.text: In the late 1800s, innovations in packaging and roasting made coffee a mass commodity for the first time.

buildup.text: Vacuum-sealed cans preserved freshness. Brands like Folgers and Maxwell House reached every household.

discovery.text: Instant coffee, invented in 1901, made brewing effortless. Soldiers in both world wars depended on it.

twist.text: Quality suffered. First-wave coffee prioritized convenience and price over flavor and origin.

climax.text: By the 1960s, Americans drank more coffee than ever—but most of it was weak, bitter, and generic.

punchline.text: Everyone drank coffee. Almost nobody cared how it tasted.

quiz.question: What defined first-wave coffee?
options: Mass production prioritizing convenience over quality

details.summary: The first wave of coffee, spanning the 1800s to mid-1900s, focused on mass production and convenience. Companies like Folgers and Maxwell House made coffee a household staple.
details.whyItMatters: The first wave made coffee universally accessible but reduced it to a generic commodity. It created the low bar that the second and third waves would rebel against.
takeaways: First wave focused on mass production and convenience
Folgers and Maxwell House became household names
Quality and origin were secondary to price and accessibility

faq.question: When did the first wave of coffee begin and end?
faq.answer: It broadly spans from the mid-1800s when commercial roasting and canning began through the mid-1900s. Some argue it persists today in the commodity segment. The transition to the second wave began with Peet's Coffee in 1966 and accelerated with Starbucks in the 1980s.

faq.question: What was coffee quality like during the first wave?
faq.answer: Low by modern specialty standards. Beans were often robusta or low-grade arabica, dark roasted to uniformity, pre-ground, and packaged for long shelf life. Freshness was not a priority. The goal was a consistent, inoffensive cup at the lowest possible cost.
